title: The Invention Factory: Milan to Menlo Park, the Currents, and the Grave Behind Glenmont
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Boy on the Grand Trunk Line

stops.name: Milan, Ohio, the house above the Huron
stops.date_confidence: attested. The chronology and geography lenses give coordinates about 190 m apart (41.3006 and 41.2989, same longitude); the geography value is used because that lens is anchored on the birthplace house specifically. Nothing in the pool identifies which value is the building.
stops.campa: In a small brick house on a bluff above the Huron River, Samuel and Nancy Edison have their seventh and last child and name him Thomas Alva. Milan is a grain port, its canal carrying wheat down to the lakes. Within a few years the railroad will pass the town by, the trade will die, and the family will leave. The house stays where it is, kept afterward as a museum. The boy born in it is credited with lighting the country that let this canal silt up.
sources: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park, biography
Paul Israel, Edison: A Life of Invention (1998)
suggested_refs: The Edison Birthplace Museum, Milan, Ohio, the brick cottage above the Huron River

stops.name: Port Huron, the family carried north
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in any source reached, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The family moves north to Port Huron on the St. Clair River, near Fort Gratiot, after the grain trade at Milan collapses. The boy has almost no schooling. His mother teaches him at home and he reads whatever the house holds. At about twelve his hearing begins to fail, blamed in different sources on scarlet fever and on repeated middle-ear infection; the pool does not settle which. He will keep the deafness the whole of his life. He builds the phonograph and the telephone transmitter without ever hearing either the way his customers do.
suggested_refs: The Edison family house at Fort Gratiot, Port Huron, on the St. Clair River

stops.name: Detroit, the laboratory in the baggage car
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1859-1863; the pool gives no single date, defaulted to the start of 1860, when he is about thirteen.
stops.campa: At thirteen he sells newspapers and candy on the Grand Trunk line between Port Huron and Detroit, and turns a corner of the baggage car into a chemistry bench and a printing shop, setting the Grand Trunk Herald in type between stations. A fire in the car ends the arrangement and boy and equipment are put off the train. In the layovers he reads at the Detroit Young Men's Society library, later claiming to have worked through whole shelves in order. That claim rests on his own telling and on nothing else.
sources: Neil Baldwin, Edison: Inventing the Century (1995)
suggested_refs: The Grand Trunk Railway depot at Detroit and the shelves of the Detroit Young Men's Society library

stops.name: Mount Clemens, the child on the track
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The story comes from Edison and the biographers date it differently: geography gives 1862, chronology gives 1863. Geography tagged it attested, which the verification pass overruled; its own source line concedes the date is disputed. No contemporary record fixes any part of it.
stops.campa: On the platform at Mount Clemens the station agent's small son wanders in front of a rolling boxcar and the newsboy pulls him clear. J. U. MacKenzie has no money to pay for his son's life, so he pays in telegraphy, teaching the boy the key over the following months. Every version of this comes from Edison, told long afterward, and the biographers cannot agree on the year. The trade it gives him is real whatever the story is worth. It carries him off the Michigan line and into the wire offices between Ontario and Tennessee, and it is the one trade a deaf boy with no schooling can enter on his hands alone.
suggested_refs: The Mount Clemens railroad station and J. U. MacKenzie's telegraph key

stops.name: Stratford, Ontario, the signal six
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Geography dates the posting 1862-1863 and tagged it attested; the verification pass demoted it. The hourly signal, the rigged sender, and the near collision all descend from Edison's own retelling decades later, with no contemporary documentation. Biographers repeat it as he told it.
stops.campa: Night operator at the Grand Trunk office, sixteen years old, he is required to send the signal 6 down the wire every hour to prove he is awake. He builds a notched wheel onto the clock to send it for him and sleeps through his watch; two trains nearly meet head on, and he leaves the job under pressure. Nothing written at the time records any of it. The first machine he is remembered for building stands in for a man on night duty, and the man is himself.
suggested_refs: The Grand Trunk Railway telegraph office at Stratford, Ontario

stops.name: Louisville, the acid through the floor
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1866-1867; the pool gives no month, defaulted to January 1866.
stops.campa: He drifts office to office, Cincinnati, Memphis, Indianapolis, working nights, reading, taking instruments apart in the hours when the traffic is thin. At Indianapolis he rigs an automatic repeater to slow incoming press copy to a speed his hand can follow. At Louisville he works the Western Union night desk until a jar of sulfuric acid goes over, burns through the floorboards, and lands on his manager's desk in the room below. He is dismissed. The pattern is set by now: hired for the hand, discharged for the experiments.
suggested_refs: The Western Union night office at Louisville, Kentucky; the Indianapolis automatic repeater

stops.name: Boston, the shop on Court Street
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1868-1869; the arrival month is not in the pool, defaulted to January. The patent grant date of 1 June 1869 is attested exactly and is given in the campa.
stops.campa: He comes east to Western Union in Boston and spends his free hours at Charles Williams Jr.'s instrument shop, 109 Court Street, where he builds the first thing he ever patents: an electrographic vote recorder, granted 1 June 1869 as United States Patent 90,646. It works. No legislature wants it, because a legislature's minority lives by the slow roll call. He is twenty-two, and he never again builds a thing before establishing that somebody will pay for it.
suggested_refs: Charles Williams Jr.'s instrument shop, 109 Court Street, Boston, where the telephone was also built

segments.name: Broad Street and the Ward Street Shops

stops.name: New York, the transmitter that failed at 42 Broad Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January. The founding of the firm with Franklin Leonard Pope is separately attested to October 1869 and is given in the campa.
stops.campa: He arrives in New York with no money and, by the account he gave afterward, is standing in the offices of the Law Gold Indicator Company when the central transmitter fails and the floor fills with panicking messenger boys. He repairs it in front of the management and is hired. In October he founds a telegraph engineering firm with Franklin Leonard Pope. Within two years Western Union pays him about forty thousand dollars for improvements gathered into the Universal Stock Printer, and he stops working for other men.
stops.quote: Everything comes to him who hustles while he waits.
stops.quote_source: Edison, quoted in Francis Arthur Jones, Thomas Alva Edison: Sixty Years of an Inventor's Life (1908), p. 14
suggested_refs: Law's Gold Indicator Company, 42 Broad Street, New York

stops.name: Newark, the Ward Street shops
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1870-1875; the pool gives no month for the opening, defaulted to January 1871. The marriage date of 25 December 1871 is attested exactly and is given in the campa.
stops.campa: With the stock printer money he opens shops on Ward Street employing dozens of machinists, and for five years Newark makes tickers, printers, and telegraph instruments to his design and under his hand. On Christmas Day 1871 he marries Mary Stilwell, lately one of his own employees; they will have three children. He is a manufacturer now, with a payroll and a shop floor, and he is finding out that he would rather run the laboratory than the factory that pays for it.
suggested_refs: The Edison manufacturing shops on Ward Street, Newark, New Jersey

stops.name: London, the Central Telegraph Office
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He crosses to London to sell his automatic telegraph to the British Post Office and demonstrates it in the Central Telegraph Office before the officials who run the largest wire network on earth. The system works on the short American lines. On the long British circuits the induction smears his signals, and he does not get the contract he came for. He goes home without the business. It is his first sight of the capital he will electrify nine years later, ahead of New York.
suggested_refs: The Central Telegraph Office, London, and the British Post Office automatic telegraph trials of 1873

stops.name: Newark, the quadruplex sold
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He completes the quadruplex, which carries four messages down one wire at once, two in each direction, and sells it for about thirty thousand dollars. Western Union and Jay Gould both want it and the ownership ends in litigation. The money matters more than the lawsuit. It buys the thing he has wanted since the vote recorder taught him what a shop floor costs: ground out in the country, a building of his own, and men paid to do nothing at all but invent.
suggested_refs: The quadruplex telegraph and the Western Union litigation of 1874-1875

stops.name: Menlo Park, the laboratory in the fields
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January. Coordinate corrected: the chronology lens gave 40.5576, -74.3396 and the geography lens 40.5701, -74.4149, about 6.4 km apart. The documented site, marked by the Edison Memorial Tower at 37 Christie St, is 40.5631, -74.3394, used here and at every later Menlo Park stop.
stops.campa: He builds at a rail crossroads twenty-five miles from New York a laboratory that exists for no product and no customer: machine shop below, benches and a chemical stock above, staffed by machinists, chemists, and glassblowers working to his direction. It is the first industrial research laboratory. He promises a minor invention every ten days and a big thing every six months. Within a year the carbon transmitter comes out of it and the telephone becomes audible over distance, because the thing Bell built could be heard only when shouted into.
suggested_refs: The Menlo Park laboratory buildings, later dismantled and shipped to Greenfield Village, Michigan

stops.name: Menlo Park, the tinfoil phonograph
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1877; no day in the pool, defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: Working on a telegraph repeater that embosses dots into paper tape, he notices the tape sings when it runs fast under the stylus. He hands John Kruesi a drawing of a grooved brass cylinder wrapped in tinfoil with a diaphragm and needle at either end. The machine speaks back on the first trial. Nothing before it has ever held a voice. Alexander Graham Bell, whose telephone Edison has just made carry, answers within a decade from the Volta Laboratory in Washington with a wax cylinder in place of the tinfoil, and the long argument over recorded sound opens between them.
suggested_refs: Kruesi's first tinfoil phonograph, Menlo Park, November 1877

stops.name: New York, the office of the Scientific American
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the journal itself. The coordinate is a placeholder: the corpus's canonical New York pin is used because the office address for December 1877 is not in the pool with a coordinate. Geography wrongly placed this demonstration at the Menlo Park laboratory; the journal's own text puts it in its New York office.
stops.campa: He carries the machine into the office of the Scientific American on the seventh of December and sets it on the editors' desk, and the room fills until the floor is judged unsafe. The demonstration that makes him famous happens here, in a New York editorial office, not at Menlo Park where the retelling has since put it. The recitation of Mary Had a Little Lamb belongs to a re-enactment he staged in 1927 for the cameras. No cylinder from 1877 was preserved, and what the machine said that winter survives only in the words of the men who heard it.
stops.quote: a young man came into the office of the Scientific American and placed before the editors a small, simple machine
stops.quote_source: Scientific American, 22 December 1877, reporting the demonstration of 7 December
suggested_refs: Scientific American, 22 December 1877, the first printed account of the phonograph

stops.name: Washington, the phonograph before President Hayes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: He demonstrates the phonograph to the National Academy of Sciences and then, late on the night of the eighteenth of April, to President Rutherford B. Hayes at the White House. Hayes wakes his wife to hear it. The machine has no commercial market and will not have one for another decade, and it is at this moment the most famous object in the United States. He is thirty-one and deaf, and he is about to put it away for four years to solve electric light instead.
suggested_refs: The White House phonograph demonstration of 18 April 1878

stops.name: New York, Drexel, Morgan and Company at 23 Wall Street
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the pool gives no month. November is the conventional incorporation date of the Edison Electric Light Company and is carried here as reconstruction, not as an attested date.
stops.campa: At 23 Wall Street the house of Drexel, Morgan and Company, with the Vanderbilts, puts up the capital for the Edison Electric Light Company. Edison has not yet made a lamp that burns. He has made a promise in the newspapers that he will divide electric light into small units and sell it to houses by the meter, and the promise alone is enough for the strongest bank in America. J. P. Morgan buys into the lighting of the world before the light exists. He will still hold the paper when the company carrying Edison's name is renamed without it.
suggested_refs: Drexel, Morgan & Co., 23 Wall Street, and the incorporation of the Edison Electric Light Company

stops.name: Menlo Park, the carbonized filament
stops.date_confidence: the date is the canonical one and is carried, but geography tags the whole breakthrough as reconstruction: Israel (1998) treats the single clean date as a commemorative construction popularized decades later for Light's Golden Jubilee, and the laboratory notebooks show incremental tests through the autumn of 1879. The patent filing of 4 November 1879 and the grant of 27 January 1880 are attested exactly.
stops.campa: After a year of carbonizing everything the shop can char, a filament of carbonized cotton thread in a high vacuum burns through the twenty-first of October and on into the next day. He files on the fourth of November for the improved electric lamp, granted as Patent 223,898, and lights the Menlo Park grounds for the public at Christmas so that visitors come out by special train to see a street burning without flame. The clean single date is a later construction. The notebooks show a whole autumn of tests, none of them a moment.
suggested_refs: U.S. Patent 223,898, filed 4 November 1879, granted 27 January 1880

stops.name: New York, 65 Fifth Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January. The Edison Illuminating Company's charter date of 17 December 1880 is attested exactly and is given in the campa.
stops.campa: He moves his office and the headquarters of the lighting company to 65 Fifth Avenue, and the Edison Machine Works to Goerck Street on the Lower East Side, where the dynamos are built. The Edison Illuminating Company was chartered on the seventeenth of December 1880 to build and run the stations. The inventing is finished; what remains is a utility. He is running manufacture, finance, and supply out of a New York address now, with Menlo Park behind him and emptying.
suggested_refs: The Edison Electric Light Company offices, 65 Fifth Avenue, New York

stops.name: London, the Holborn Viaduct station
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1882; no day in the pool, defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: The Holborn Viaduct station is switched on in January, ninety-three kilowatts of steam-driven generation feeding street lamps and the buildings along the viaduct, among the earliest public electricity supplies anywhere. London gets the demonstration plant nine years after refusing his automatic telegraph. It runs about four years and closes. The plant earns him an income statement to carry into the City of London, and he wants it in hand before he goes to Wall Street for the capital to build the same thing larger.
suggested_refs: The Holborn Viaduct generating station, London, January 1882

stops.name: New York, the banker's house on Madison Avenue
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month is not in the pool and June is carried as reconstruction. The two lenses give coordinates about 300 m apart (geography 40.7488, -73.9822; afterlife 40.7484, -73.9857); the geography value is used and the disagreement is not resolved.
stops.campa: Edison's men run wires through the mansion at 219 Madison Avenue and set a generator in a shed behind it, and J. P. Morgan's house becomes one of the first private houses in the world lit by incandescent lamps. The installation is a showroom as much as a convenience: the men who dine at that table are the men whose capital the central stations will need. Ten years on, the same host will merge the company out from under its founder's name without asking him.
sources: Rutgers Edison Papers Project, institutional summaries
suggested_refs: J. P. Morgan's residence, 219 Madison Avenue, wired in 1882

stops.name: New York, Pearl Street Station
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Customer figures corrected: the chronology lens gave 946 customers at opening, which matches no documented figure; geography independently gave roughly 85, which is close to the documented 82. Coordinate corrected from both lenses to the documented 40.7078, -74.0047.
stops.campa: The switch closes at Pearl Street and six dynamos push a hundred and ten volts of direct current into a square mile of lower Manhattan. The first load is four hundred lamps for eighty-two customers; by 1884 it is five hundred and eight customers and ten thousand one hundred and sixty-four lamps. It is the first commercial central generating station in the United States. Direct current will not carry much beyond a mile from the plant, and that one limit is the whole of what happens next.
suggested_refs: Pearl Street Station, lower Manhattan, and the six jumbo dynamos of 1882

stops.name: New York, the Goerck Street works and the Serb with Batchelor's letter
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1884 for the landing; no day for the hiring, defaulted to the first. The resignation is attested to December 1884.
stops.campa: A Serb of twenty-eight lands at Castle Garden in June carrying a letter of introduction from Charles Batchelor, Edison's closest hand, and is put to work the same night on a steamer's dynamos. Nikola Tesla stays about six months at the Goerck Street works redesigning the direct-current machines Edison sells. He resigns in December over a bonus Edison declines to pay, calling it, by Tesla's account, American humor. Tesla had already served the Continental Edison Company at Paris and Strasbourg. He leaves here with the polyphase system in his head and nowhere to build it.
stops.quote: Good By to the Edison Machine Works
stops.quote_source: Tesla's diary, December 1884; Tesla, My Inventions, Ch. IV (via nikola_tesla.journey.json)
suggested_refs: The Edison Machine Works, Goerck Street, New York, where Tesla worked six months in 1884

stops.name: Schenectady, the works moved to the canal
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; no month in the pool, December carried as reconstruction so that the move sits after the Akron marriage of February 1886. The quotation carried here is dated November 1886.
stops.campa: He moves the Machine Works off the crowded Lower East Side to unfinished buildings on the Erie Canal at Schenectady, for cheap land and rail access. Within six years the site is the manufacturing core of General Electric. In the same year George Westinghouse begins building alternating-current plants, whose transformers carry power at high voltage over distances direct current cannot reach, and Edison, who has staked his whole system on a hundred and ten volts and a one-mile radius, starts telling anyone who will print it that the other current kills.
stops.quote: Just as certain as death, Westinghouse will kill a customer within six months after he puts in a system of any size. He has got a new thing and it will require a great deal of experimenting to get it working practically.
stops.quote_source: Edison, letter to Edward H. Johnson, November 1886; quoted in Maury Klein, The Power Makers (2010), p. 257
suggested_refs: The Edison Machine Works at Schenectady, later the core plant of General Electric

stops.name: West Orange, the animals and the chair
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Year corrected: the chronology lens dated the Brown campaign 1887, but every documented event in it falls in 1888, the Post letter on 5 June, the Columbia College dog on 30 July, a second on 3 August, the horse and calf at West Orange on 5 December.
stops.campa: Harold P. Brown, an electrical engineer given the run of Edison's laboratory, writes to the New York Post in June that alternating current is fit only for killing, electrocutes a dog before an audience at Columbia College in July, and on the fifth of December kills a horse and a calf with Westinghouse machines in Edison's own West Orange laboratory, before witnesses from the New York death-penalty commission. Edison has already written to the commission naming whose machines will do it. The state adopts the chair.
stops.quote: alternating machines, manufactured principally in this country by Geo. Westinghouse
stops.quote_source: Edison, letter to Alfred P. Southwick, December 1887; quoted in Jill Jonnes, Empires of Light (2003), p. 420
suggested_refs: Harold P. Brown's letter to the New York Post, 5 June 1888, and the West Orange electrocutions of 5 December 1888

stops.name: New York, the name struck off the company
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the pool gives no month, April carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: J. P. Morgan merges Edison General Electric with its rival Thomson-Houston and the founder's name comes off the door. The new company is General Electric, holding roughly three quarters of the American electrical business, and Edison is neither its president nor a director of it. Thomson-Houston builds alternating current. The merger settles the war by swallowing both sides, and the man who spent six years arguing that the other current was lethal holds shares in a firm that sells it.
suggested_refs: The 1892 Morgan merger of Edison General Electric and Thomson-Houston into General Electric

stops.name: Chicago, the White City lit by the other current
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fair, which opened 1 May 1893. Whether Edison himself walked the grounds is not established by anything in the research pool and is not asserted. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from nikola_tesla.journey.json.
stops.campa: Westinghouse underbids General Electric and lights the World's Columbian Exposition with the polyphase alternating current of Nikola Tesla, whom Edison's works dismissed nine years earlier over a bonus. It is the public verdict in the War of the Currents and it goes against direct current entirely. Edison's companies exhibit at the fair among the rest. The same ground carries Muybridge showing moving pictures and Vivekananda addressing the Parliament of Religions: the White City is a crossroads several roads in this atlas run through in one summer.
sources: nikola_tesla.journey.json (Chicago, the White City lit by his system)
suggested_refs: The World's Columbian Exposition, Jackson Park, Chicago, lit by Westinghouse and Tesla in 1893

stops.name: Menlo Park, the death of Mary Stilwell
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Place corrected: the chronology lens hedged the place as 'Menlo Park or New York' and then attached Newark's coordinate, which matches neither; the verification pass places the death at the Menlo Park house.
stops.campa: Mary Stilwell Edison dies at the Menlo Park house on the ninth of August, twenty-nine years old, thirteen years married, leaving three children. He is thirty-seven and in the middle of the fight over the currents. The sources gathered here do not even agree on where she died, some saying Menlo Park and some New York. He shuts the house. The laboratory that made his name is already half emptied into Manhattan, and from this month it is done with. The widower goes looking for a new wife and a new laboratory at the same time.
suggested_refs: The Menlo Park residence, closed after Mary Stilwell Edison's death in August 1884

stops.name: Fort Myers, the land on the Caloosahatchee
stops.date_confidence: the estate's own history dates the first visit and the purchase to 1885 and the completed house to 1886; the geography lens dated the purchase 1886, which the verification pass corrected. No month is documented, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He comes down to the Caloosahatchee River in southwest Florida and buys land on the south bank; the winter house is finished the following year. Seminole Lodge is a residence with a laboratory attached, which is the only kind of house he builds. The climate brings him down, and the plants that grow in it keep him returning every winter for the rest of his life. The estate's own history dates the purchase to 1885 and the finished house to 1886, which is not how the chronologies usually give it. Forty-three years later this same ground holds the last experiment of his life, and Henry Ford owns the lot next door.
sources: Edison and Ford Winter Estates, official history
suggested_refs: Seminole Lodge, Fort Myers, Florida, the winter house and laboratory on the Caloosahatchee

stops.name: West Orange, Glenmont bought before the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, January carried so that the purchase precedes the February wedding. Coordinate corrected: chronology gave 40.7987, -74.2391, about 1.4 km north in generic West Orange, and the afterlife lens gave 40.7855, -74.2313, about 790 m east; the documented Glenmont is 40.7861, -74.2406.
stops.campa: In Llewellyn Park, a gated woodland suburb on the ridge above West Orange, he buys Glenmont, a house of twenty-nine rooms, as the setting for a marriage not yet made. He will live in it forty-five years, die in it at eighty-four, and lie buried on its lawn from 1963 onward. The laboratory goes up a mile downhill the following year. He crosses between the ridge and the works for forty-four years, and the second half of his life happens along that mile.
sources: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park
suggested_refs: Glenmont, Llewellyn Park, West Orange, New Jersey

stops.name: Akron, Oak Place and Mina Miller
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: He marries Mina Miller at Oak Place, her father's house in Akron, on the twenty-fourth of February. Lewis Miller invents farm machinery and founded the Chautauqua assembly, so the bride is educated and the family is not impressed by fame by itself. Edison, deaf, courted her by teaching her Morse and tapping into her palm. She is twenty and he is thirty-nine, and she will run Glenmont for the next forty-five years and be buried beside him behind it.
suggested_refs: Oak Place, the Miller family house at Akron, Ohio

stops.name: West Orange, the laboratory ten times larger
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1887; no day in the pool, defaulted to the first. Coordinate corrected from the geography lens's 40.7889, -74.2379, about 700 m off, to the documented 40.7836, -74.2336.
stops.campa: A mile downhill from Glenmont he opens a laboratory complex ten times the size of Menlo Park: a three-storey main building with a library, machine shops, and stock rooms holding by his own instruction every material a man might want, and satellite buildings for chemistry, physics, metallurgy, and pattern-making. Charles Batchelor oversees the construction. Invention and manufacture now sit on one site, under one roof and one payroll, and the plant runs for forty-four years.
sources: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park
suggested_refs: The West Orange laboratory complex, now Thomas Edison National Historical Park

stops.name: Paris, the Exposition Universelle on the Champ de Mars
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1889; no day in the pool, defaulted to the first. The interlock lens suggested collapsing this to the corpus's canonical Paris pin, 48.8566, 2.3522, but that was tagged as reconstruction and is not done: his attested location is the Champ de Mars.
stops.campa: He crosses to the Exposition Universelle on the Champ de Mars, where his phonograph and lighting exhibits take a large part of the American section and draw crowds all summer. Gustave Eiffel takes him up the new tower to the apartment at the top. He is received across Europe on the same trip much as a head of state would be. Seven years earlier a young draftsman named Tesla was repairing the Continental Edison Company's lighting plants in this city, for a firm that carried Edison's name and had never seen him.
suggested_refs: The Edison exhibit at the Exposition Universelle, Paris, 1889

stops.name: West Orange, the Black Maria
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January. Coordinate corrected from the geography lens's 40.7895, -74.2385, about 700 m off, to the documented 40.7842, -74.2336.
stops.campa: In the yard at West Orange, for six hundred and thirty-seven dollars and sixty-seven cents, he puts up a shed covered in tar paper with a roof that opens to the sky and a track beneath the whole building so it can be turned to follow the sun. The men call it the Black Maria, after the police wagon. William Kennedy Dickson has been building the camera and the peephole viewer here since 1891. It is the first building in the world made for producing motion pictures, and the following April a parlour at 1155 Broadway sells the first tickets.
sources: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park
Charles Musser, The Emergence of Cinema (1990)
suggested_refs: The Black Maria studio, West Orange, and the Kinetoscope parlour at 1155 Broadway, opened 14 April 1894

stops.name: West Orange, the fluoroscope and Clarence Dally
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January. Dates disentangled: the chronology lens conflated the abandonment of the work, about 1903, with Dally's injury. Dally's arms were amputated and he died on 2 October 1904.
stops.campa: Rontgen's paper reaches him and within weeks he has a fluoroscope working, a calcium tungstate screen that makes the new rays visible without a plate, and he refuses to patent it. Clarence Dally, the glassblower who holds his own hands in the beam day after day to test the tubes, loses first his hair, then his hands, then his arms, and dies in 1904. Edison, his own eyesight damaged, stops the work about 1903 and will not touch X-rays again. Dally is generally counted the first American killed by a man-made radiation source.
suggested_refs: Edison's calcium tungstate fluoroscope, never patented, and the death of Clarence Dally, 2 October 1904

stops.name: New Village, Stewartsville, the cement works
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January. Coordinate corrected: the chronology lens attached West Orange to this company; the works were at New Village, Stewartsville, Warren County.
stops.campa: Ten years of his own fortune went into a magnetic ore separation works in the hills at Ogdensburg, crushing low-grade New Jersey iron with rock-breakers of his own design, until Mesabi ore out of Minnesota undercut the price and the venture closed with nothing recovered. He carries the crushing and kiln machinery west across the state to New Village and makes Portland cement with it, in the longest rotary kilns then working. Out of the wreck of the iron mine he will pour cement houses, cement furniture, and a stadium in the Bronx.
suggested_refs: The Edison ore-milling works at Ogdensburg and the Edison Portland Cement works at New Village, New Jersey

stops.name: West Orange, ten thousand cells
stops.date_confidence: the research is attested from 1899 and the patents and the founding of the Edison Storage Battery Company to 1901; no month in the pool, defaulted to January 1901.
stops.campa: He sets the West Orange chemistry building to a rechargeable cell for electric road vehicles, nickel and iron in alkali to replace lead in acid, and works through something on the order of ten thousand combinations of electrode and electrolyte. He patents it in the United States and Europe in 1901 and founds the Edison Storage Battery Company. The petrol engine takes the automobile anyway. The cell survives in mine lamps, signal lanterns, and submarines, and it is the most profitable thing he ever makes.
stops.quote: Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration.
stops.quote_source: Edison, 1927 letter reproduced in the Argus Leader, 21 February 1932, p. 18; also printed in Harper's Monthly, September 1932
suggested_refs: The Edison nickel-iron alkaline cell and the Edison Storage Battery Company, 1901

stops.name: West Orange, the fire
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1914; the pool gives no day, defaulted to the first, and the commonly cited ninth of December is not asserted here.
stops.campa: Fire takes hold at the West Orange plant on a December night and thirteen buildings burn, one employee dead, about a million and a half dollars destroyed. He has the rubble cleared at once and record manufacture resumes within weeks. He is sixty-seven. Three years earlier he had folded every one of his manufacturing companies into Thomas A. Edison Incorporated with himself as president and chairman, so what burns is his own and what goes up in its place is his own, and he builds it larger than it was.
suggested_refs: The West Orange fire of December 1914 and the reconstruction of the plant

stops.name: Washington, the Naval Consulting Board
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The Navy asks him to head a board of civilian inventors to bring American industry into the war Europe is already fighting, and he takes it, seating a member from each of the national engineering societies. He proposes some forty devices, most of them defensive: submarine detection, ship camouflage, torpedo evasion. The Navy adopts almost none of them while the war lasts. The board's one lasting product is the Naval Research Laboratory, which is his idea, and which is Menlo Park again with the government paying the wages.
suggested_refs: The Naval Consulting Board, 1915, and the founding of the Naval Research Laboratory

stops.name: Fort Myers, the goldenrod laboratory
stops.date_confidence: the geography lens dates the Botanic Research laboratory 1928 and the chronology lens dates the rubber project 1927; both are carried and the discrepancy is not resolved. No month in either, defaulted to January. The Congressional Gold Medal is attested to 1928.
stops.campa: Henry Ford and Harvey Firestone put up the money and Edison, eighty-one, takes the last problem: a rubber plant that will grow inside the United States, against the day a blockade cuts the country off from Malaya and Brazil. He tests hundreds of species at the Fort Myers laboratory and settles on goldenrod, breeding it taller and taller until the leaf gives usable latex. Congress votes him the Gold Medal the same year. He is still at the goldenrod when he dies.
stops.quote: It is absurd to say that our country can issue $30,000,000 in bonds and not $30,000,000 in currency. Both are promises to pay, but one promise fattens the usurer and the other helps the people.
stops.quote_source: Edison at Muscle Shoals with Henry Ford, New York Times, 6 December 1921
sources: Edison and Ford Winter Estates, official history
suggested_refs: The Edison Botanic Research Corporation laboratory, Fort Myers, and the goldenrod rubber trials

stops.name: Dearborn, Light's Golden Jubilee
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinate corrected: the chronology lens gave 42.3223, -83.1763, about 5 km off into northeast Dearborn; Greenfield Village is at 42.3036, -83.2342. The geography lens's 42.308, -83.2352 agrees with the corrected value to within 200 m.
stops.campa: Henry Ford has taken the Menlo Park laboratory apart in New Jersey, shipped the buildings to Michigan, and rebuilt them at Greenfield Village. On the fiftieth anniversary of the lamp, before President Herbert Hoover, Edison sits at the reconstructed bench where he sat at thirty-two and re-enacts the making of the filament. He is eighty-two and in poor health. The evening is called Light's Golden Jubilee, and it is the ceremony that fixes the twenty-first of October 1879 in the national calendar as a single dated event it never was.
stops.quote: We don't know a millionth of one percent about anything.
stops.quote_source: Edison, quoted in Golden Book Magazine, April 1931
suggested_refs: The reconstructed Menlo Park laboratory at Greenfield Village, Dearborn, Michigan

stops.name: West Orange, Glenmont, the last morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The hour is contradicted between sources: the National Park Service gives 3:21 a.m. and the afterlife lens carried 3:24 a.m. Both are printed in the campa and neither is preferred.
stops.campa: He dies at Glenmont in the early morning of the eighteenth of October, eighty-four years old, after months of failing from complications of diabetes. The Park Service gives the hour as 3:21; other accounts give 3:24. Henry Ford is said to have had a test tube held at the bedside to catch the last breath, and a sealed tube is on display at Ford's museum in Dearborn to this day. Whether anything was caught in it, or whether the tube merely stood in the room, no medical record settles.
sources: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park
Henry Ford Museum object records (disputed by biographers)
suggested_refs: The sealed test tube attributed to Edison's last breath, Henry Ford Museum, Dearborn

stops.name: Orange, Rosedale Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the burial; 21 October is the date given for the national dimming of lights on the night of the funeral, and is used for the stop. The extent of the dimming is disputed.
stops.campa: He is buried at Rosedale Cemetery in Orange, three days after his death. On the evening of the funeral the country is asked to dim its lights, and utilities and cities across the United States cut or lower current for a minute; the accounts differ on how general it was, some describing a coordinated national blackout and others a patchy voluntary gesture. Two days before, the New York papers had printed the assessment of Nikola Tesla, which is less an obituary than the last word in a quarrel begun on Goerck Street.
stops.quote: Edison was by far the most successful and, probably, the last exponent of the purely empirical method of investigation. His method was inefficient in the extreme, for an immense ground had to be covered to get anything at all unless blind chance intervened.
stops.quote_source: Nikola Tesla, 'Tesla Says Edison Was an Empiricist,' New York Times, 19 October 1931, p. 25
sources: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park
Contemporary newspaper accounts of October 1931 (extent disputed)
suggested_refs: Rosedale Cemetery, Orange, New Jersey, the first grave

stops.name: Edison, New Jersey, the tower on the empty ground
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, his ninety-first birthday. Coordinate corrected: the afterlife lens gave 40.5292, -74.3399, about 3.8 km too far south; the documented tower stands at 40.5631, -74.3394, the same pin used for the Menlo Park laboratory stops.
stops.campa: On the ground where the Menlo Park laboratory stood, on what would have been his ninety-first birthday, a concrete shaft a hundred and thirty-one feet high is dedicated with a Pyrex bulb thirteen feet eight inches tall on top of it. The buildings themselves are in Michigan. The tower marks an absence: it stands where the invention factory stood before Ford carried it away, and its light burns over an empty field in a New Jersey township that renamed itself Edison.
suggested_refs: The Edison Memorial Tower, 37 Christie Street, Edison, New Jersey, dedicated 11 February 1938

stops.name: West Orange, Glenmont, the lawn behind the house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no month in the pool, defaulted to January. The laboratory's reopening after restoration is attested to 10 October 2009. The statue in the National Statuary Hall Collection is attested to 2016; the afterlife lens added a May installation that neither source supports, and the month is dropped.
stops.campa: Thirty-two years after the funeral he and Mina are lifted out of Rosedale and reburied in a small fenced plot on the lawn behind Glenmont, inside what is now Thomas Edison National Historical Park. The house is kept as it stood. The laboratory a mile downhill reopens in October 2009 after a long restoration, the library still holding the cot he slept on between shifts. In 2016 Ohio takes down its statue of William Allen in the Capitol and puts up one of him, which is how a country revises a wall of names.
sources: National Park Service, Thomas Edison National Historical Park
Architect of the Capitol, National Statuary Hall Collection
suggested_refs: The Edison graves on the Glenmont lawn, and the Edison statue in the National Statuary Hall Collection, 2016
